tldr: In reinforcement learning for quadruped robots, the proposed framework "CARO" intentionally uses a simplified fixed-base dynamics model to estimate torque residuals and feeds them into the policy as observations. Without relying on force/torque sensors, contact estimation, or base velocity measurements, it enables zero-shot robust adaptation to extreme out-of-distribution payloads, unseen rough terrains, and abrupt payload additions during locomotion.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of CARO. A fixed-base Euler–Lagrange internal model and a disturbance observer are integrated into the reinforcement learning control loop, feeding discrepancies against commanded torques into the policy as residual observations. A key feature is that the estimated residual is provided to the policy as an adaptive input signal rather than applied directly as feedforward torque compensation.
overview:
While reinforcement learning (RL) has significantly advanced quadruped locomotion, robustness against "unseen environments" outside the simulator's training distribution remains a major challenge. When faced with heavy payloads not seen during training or suddenly entering severely uneven terrain, robots frequently lose their footing and fall.

To tackle this, the authors focused on the "discrepancy in model prediction (residual)." Monitoring the difference between joint torque commands and the behavior predicted by a nominal dynamics model should allow quick detection of external forces and terrain changes. However, quadruped robots are floating-base systems that move freely in space with frequently switching contacts. Computing a rigorous model requires accurate base velocity estimation, force sensors, and contact detection, making real-world deployment extremely difficult.

In response to this dilemma, CARO (Contact-Agnostic Residual Observation) takes a bold, simplifying approach: it intentionally assumes a fixed-base Euler–Lagrange model. While giving up on estimating contact forces directly, it captures the combined effects of disturbances and loads transmitted back through the feet into the joints as a lumped residual and passes it to the policy as an observation.

Experimental results show that CARO exhibits outstanding resilience against payloads up to three times the base mass, unseen rough terrains, and sudden payload additions during locomotion (adding 50% of the robot's body weight)—all without specialized disturbance curricula. Furthermore, in real-world experiments on a DeepRobotics Lite3, it achieved zero-shot success in maintaining straight-line walking under asymmetric eccentric loading and landing stably after jumping off an elevated platform.
contributions: Proposed a lightweight residual observer based on a fixed-base model that can be deployed on real hardware without force/torque sensors, base velocity estimation, or explicit contact estimation.
Leveraged estimated joint torque residuals as structured observation inputs for policy adaptation in contact-rich environments, rather than using them for direct torque compensation.

Achieved substantial zero-shot robustness in both simulation and real hardware using only training on flat terrain with nominal domain randomization, without specialized disturbance curricula or additional adaptation supervision.

sections.heading: Why Do Quadruped Robots Fail in Out-of-Distribution Environments?
sections.summary: Although RL-based quadruped locomotion has achieved remarkable agility, robustness in out-of-distribution environments remains a bottleneck. This section highlights the limitations of existing implicit adaptation modules and model-based methods, introducing the core idea and motivation behind CARO's simplified internal model residual observation.
sections.details:
Reinforcement learning has endowed quadruped robots with extraordinary motor capabilities. Impressive feats such as high-speed sprinting and traversing rough terrains have been reported, yet deep-seated robustness issues persist when deploying these policies in real-world environments. When faced with severe conditions exceeding simulator assumptions, policy performance drops drastically.

Most existing methods rely on domain randomization (training across randomly perturbed physical parameters in simulation) or adaptation modules like RMA that infer environmental parameters as latent variables from past observation histories. While effective for moderate distribution shifts, these lack a physically structured feedback path capable of capturing abrupt contact transitions and sudden dynamics changes.

On the other hand, attempts to incorporate control-theoretic model-based approaches (such as disturbance observers) face hurdles: legged robots are hybrid, non-linear systems with discontinuous contact switches. Solving exact floating-base inverse dynamics requires precise base position/velocity estimation, foot contact wrench (forces and torques) estimation, and actuator modeling, making them extremely fragile in real-world environments with severe foot slip and impacts.

To address this, CARO (Contact-Agnostic Residual Observation) was proposed. It integrates a fixed-base Euler–Lagrange model into the RL control loop, intentionally assuming the torso is fixed. Even when omitting base dynamics, external forces, payload changes, and terrain irregularities inevitably manifest as joint torque discrepancies through contact forces. By detecting these discrepancies without force sensors and feeding them as adaptive signals to the policy, CARO enables robust locomotion under unseen payloads and terrain variations.

sections.heading: History-Based Adaptation vs. Disturbance Observers: Key Differences from Prior Work
sections.summary: This section reviews adaptation methods in RL locomotion (such as RMA and RL2AC) and disturbance observer lineages for legged robots. CARO distinguishes itself by not seeking precise identification of contact forces or base velocities, intentionally delegating lumped joint-space residuals to the policy as observations.
sections.details:
This section organizes prior work into two main categories:

- Robustification Methods in RL Locomotion:
Representative approaches like RMA (Rapid Motor Adaptation) and DreamWaQ estimate latent environmental features from histories of proprioceptive measurements (joint angles, angular velocities, etc.). However, these are implicit history estimators lacking dynamically structured residual feedback. Meanwhile, methods combining adaptive controllers like RL2AC demand real-world torque sensors, and Neural-IMC requires floating-base state estimation, posing high hardware demands.

- Disturbance Estimation in Legged Robots:
Approaches using momentum observers to estimate external forces (such as ADAPT and MOB-Net) have been extensively studied in manipulators and humanoids. However, most aim to physically identify accurate contact forces or external torques to directly inject feedforward compensation torques. Consequently, they require precise base velocity estimation or two-stage learning pipelines.

CARO's stance is fundamentally different. Instead of attempting exact contact identification or direct torque compensation, it feeds a coarse yet dynamically structured residual from a fixed-base approximation directly to the policy as an observation. Entrusting the policy's adaptive capability to interpret what is happening minimizes sensor requirements while enabling zero-shot adaptation to unknown loads.

sections.heading: The Counterintuitive "Fixed-Base" Assumption and Observer Mathematics
sections.summary: This section explains CARO's core algorithm. It details how the difference (residual) between commanded torques and torques derived from fixed-base equations of motion is stably estimated via a momentum-based observer without acceleration measurements, incorporated into policy observations, and proven to have bounded error.
sections.details:
Although the true equation of motion for a quadruped robot is a complex floating-base formulation, CARO adopts a fixed-base model as its internal model, assuming the torso is anchored: $\bm{M}_{\mathrm{f}}(\bm{q})\ddot{\bm{q}} + \bm{h}_{\mathrm{f}}(\bm{q},\dot{\bm{q}}) = \bm{\tau}_{\mathrm{cmd}} + \bm{r}$ (where $\bm{M}_{\mathrm{f}}$ is the inertia matrix, $\bm{h}_{\mathrm{f}}$ contains Coriolis, centrifugal, and gravity terms, $\bm{\tau}_{\mathrm{cmd}}$ is the commanded torque to PD controllers, and $\bm{r}$ is the internal model residual).

The key design choices here are using commanded torques $\bm{\tau}_{\mathrm{cmd}}$ instead of measured torques from sensors, and omitting torso accelerations as well as foot contact forces $\bm{f}_c$. Consequently, the residual $\bm{r}$ against the true system lumps together motor tracking lag, base-motion coupling terms, and foot contact forces transmitted back into the joints: $\bm{J}_{c,j}^\top \bm{f}_c$. This is why the method is named "Contact-Agnostic" (it requires no explicit contact estimation).

However, calculating $\bm{r}$ directly from this equation would require joint accelerations $\ddot{\bm{q}}$, which would fail due to sensor noise. CARO adapts the classical generalized momentum observer technique. By defining fixed-base momentum $\bm{p}_{\mathrm{f}} = \bm{M}_{\mathrm{f}}(\bm{q})\dot{\bm{q}}$ and introducing an auxiliary variable $\bm{z}$, it constructs an observer that integrates and updates the residual estimate $\hat{\bm{r}}_{\mathrm{eff}}$ without differentiating joint velocities. The only required inputs are joint positions $\bm{q}$, joint velocities $\dot{\bm{q}}$, and commanded torques $\bm{\tau}_{\mathrm{cmd}}$.

Furthermore, the paper mathematically proves as Theorem 1 that under the realistic condition of bounded step-to-step changes in residuals, the discretization estimation error $\bm{e}_k$ under forward Euler integration is ultimately bounded.

The resulting residual vector $\hat{\bm{r}}_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is concatenated with standard observations (joint positions, velocities, command velocities, etc.) and fed as additional input to the RL policy (Actor). By exposing the policy to this residual from the beginning of training, it naturally learns the dynamical context, such as recognizing that residuals on specific joints indicate load shifting to the rear legs.

captions.F1: Overall architecture of the CARO control loop. Dynamics terms calculated from the fixed-base model and commanded torques are input into the Residual Observer, and the resulting residual signal is fed back to the Policy alongside observation history.

sections.heading: Simulation and Hardware Validation: Remarkable Resilience to Overloads and Rough Terrain
sections.summary: Evaluations included out-of-distribution payload and terrain sweeps, abrupt payload drops during locomotion, and real-world experiments on a Lite3 robot covering multi-terrain traversal, eccentric loading, and platform landings. CARO substantially outperformed baseline methods in robustness and recovery.
sections.details:
Evaluations were conducted in Isaac Gym simulations and on a physical DeepRobotics Lite3 robot. Baselines included "Vanilla (standard PPO)" without adaptation mechanisms, "RMA" which estimates latent parameters from history, and "RL2AC" which combines adaptive control. Importantly, all methods were trained under identical conditions on flat terrain only, with additional payloads restricted to a narrow range of $-1.0\sim 3.0\,\mathrm{kg}$.

- Unseen Payload $\times$ Terrain Sweep:
All methods were tested across 25 combinations of 4 unseen terrains (Slope, Rough Slope, Stepping Stone, Wave) and 5 payload levels ($1.0\sim 3.0\times$ nominal base mass). CARO achieved the highest overall average success rate of $88.6\%$. In the extreme condition of $3.0\times$ base mass ($+11.2\,\mathrm{kg}$ overload), where Vanilla collapsed to $0\%$, RL2AC to $0.2\%$, and RMA to $36.4\%$, CARO maintained a $64.5\%$ success rate.

- Transient Response to Sudden Overload:
The transient response was evaluated when a $5.6\,\mathrm{kg}$ payload (approx. $50\%$ of robot mass, far exceeding the training limit of $3.0\,\mathrm{kg}$) was abruptly dropped onto the robot's back during flat-ground walking. While other methods experienced large forward velocity drops and yaw disturbances, CARO showed minimal velocity loss and recovered commanded speed almost immediately. Estimated residuals revealed sharp spikes in knee joints across all legs, especially rear legs, confirming that the policy spatially perceived load redistribution across legs and promptly corrected posture.

- Real-World Experiments (DeepRobotics Lite3):
Policies trained in simulation were directly transferred zero-shot to hardware. With a $2.5\,\mathrm{kg}$ payload, CARO successfully traversed sand, grass, gravel slopes, and stepping stones. Under an asymmetric eccentric load of $2.5\,\mathrm{kg}$ placed on one side, Vanilla experienced severe tipping and yaw drift, whereas CARO maintained a level posture and straight heading. In maximum payload tests, Vanilla fell at $6.5\,\mathrm{kg}$, while CARO continued walking up to $8.5\,\mathrm{kg}$. In drop-landing tests jumping from an elevated platform of $0.2\,\mathrm{m}$, CARO recovered stable posture without falling in $3/3$ trials.

captions.F4: Residual estimates across individual leg joints by CARO at the moment a $5.6\,\mathrm{kg}$ payload is abruptly placed on the robot's back during walking. Knee joints (green curves), especially on rear legs (RL, RR), show sharp and persistent surges, demonstrating accurate joint-space perception of load distribution.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A Simplified Internal Model Opens New Horizons for Robust Locomotion
sections.summary: By feeding torque residuals from a fixed-base model that avoids explicit contact resolution into reinforcement learning, CARO achieves high zero-shot environmental adaptability. The paper concludes that circumventing precise contact identification offers a practical design principle for robust locomotion control.
sections.details:
This paper proposed CARO, a novel observation framework enabling zero-shot adaptation for quadruped robots. Its core breakthrough lies in abandoning dependence on high-precision floating-base estimation and force sensors demanded by conventional model-based methods, focusing instead on torque residuals derived from a fixed-base Euler–Lagrange model.

Residual estimates do not physically isolate or identify individual contact states or payload masses. However, they carry sufficient structure to capture load imbalances and transient impacts within the robot's joint space. Simply feeding this signal to the policy elicits powerful adaptive reactions to abrupt dynamics changes and unseen terrains.

The high average success rate of $88.6\%$ across payload and terrain sweeps, alongside real-world successes in eccentric-load walking and elevated platform drop-landings, strongly validates the design philosophy of pairing an intentionally simplified physical model with the flexibility of learning.

sections.heading: Open Problems: Theoretical Bounds vs. Highly Dynamic Motions
sections.summary: While error boundedness is proven for the standalone observer, closed-loop stability remains unproven. This section discusses theoretical and practical limitations, including floating-base approximation errors during highly dynamic maneuvers, as well as future directions.
sections.details:
The authors highlight several limitations and open challenges for CARO:

- Lack of Full Closed-Loop Stability Guarantees:
The theoretical analysis proves step-wise error boundedness for the standalone residual observer only. Stability for the overall closed-loop control system, which includes the reinforcement learning neural network, is not mathematically guaranteed.

- Observer Gain Trade-Off:
Increasing the observer gain matrix $\bm{L}$ widens the disturbance tracking bandwidth but excessively amplifies encoder noise in joint positions and velocities. Careful tuning and filtering are necessary to suppress hardware vibrations.

- Inability to Isolate Physical Parameters and Breakdown in Dynamic Motions:
Because the residual captures all discrepancies in a lumped form, it cannot decouple specific physical parameters (e.g., determining exactly how many kilograms were added where). Furthermore, during highly dynamic motions like flips or extreme accelerations where torso acceleration dominates, the fixed-base assumption itself may break down severely and distort observations.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation Details and Practical Tricks for Sim-to-Real
sections.summary: This section summarizes practical implementation details for reproducing the work, including the observer error boundedness proof sketch, Coriolis diagonal approximations in Isaac Gym, and $50\,\mathrm{Hz}$ deployment on hardware using Pinocchio and 5-step observation histories.
sections.details:
The appendix provides mathematical and implementation details crucial for reproducing the paper:

- Proof of Theorem 1 (Appendix A):
By expanding the Euler update of the auxiliary variable $\bm{z}_k$ and solving the recurrence relation, the authors show that when gain $\bm{L}$ and sampling period $T_s$ satisfy $0 < T_s \lambda_i(\bm{L}) < 2$, the norm of the error matrix $\bm{A} = \bm{I} - T_s \bm{L}$ is strictly less than 1, establishing uniform boundedness of the estimation error.

- Fast Computation and Approximations in Simulation (Appendix C-B):
In Isaac Gym (legged_gym), computing the full fixed-base Coriolis matrix $\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}}$ was challenging due to API constraints. The authors adopted a bold diagonal approximation: $\operatorname{diag}(\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}}) = 0.1 \cdot \operatorname{diag}(\bm{M}_{\mathrm{f}})$. Even with this coarse approximation, the residual observer provided sufficiently useful adaptation signals to the policy. The sampling period matched the simulation step at $T_s = 0.02\,\mathrm{s}$ ($50\,\mathrm{Hz}$), with observer gains set uniformly to $2.0$ across all joints.

- Real Hardware Deployment:
On the physical Lite3 robot, Jacobians and inertia terms were computed using the rigid-body dynamics library "Pinocchio," executing in real time at $50\,\mathrm{Hz}$ alongside the LibTorch policy via the "rl_sar" framework. Feeding a 5-step history of observations rather than a single step proved critical for suppressing hardware-specific vibrations.

takeaways: Even for floating-base legged robots, providing joint torque residuals derived from a "fixed-base model" as observations yields powerful adaptation signals against overloads and rough terrain.

Delegating residuals to the reinforcement learning policy as observations, rather than directly applying them as feedforward torque compensation, eliminates the need for force/torque sensors or explicit contact estimation.

Even when using a coarse diagonal approximation for the Coriolis term (0.1 times $\operatorname{diag}(\bm{M})$) in simulation, the residual observer functions effectively and transfers successfully to hardware.
Without specialized disturbance curricula or two-stage training, policies achieve extreme out-of-distribution zero-shot robustness purely through nominal domain randomization on flat ground.
limitations: While observer estimation error is bounded, closed-loop stability encompassing the policy network is not theoretically guaranteed.
In highly dynamic motions where torso accelerations become extreme (e.g., jumps or flips), breakdown of the fixed-base assumption may severely corrupt residual observations.
The residual represents a lumped sum of external forces, model mismatch, and actuator lag; it cannot disentangle individual physical parameters such as exact mass values or contact locations.
